https://www.wral.com/news/ap/1d5a2-eston.text: This ethnic community in Estonia turns a village into a symbolic kingdom for a day MIKITAMÄE, Estonia (AP) — As an accordion plays, 80-year-old Maime Kapten spins across the grass field, her embroidered skirt swirling and silver chains and coins around her neck jangling. Posted 8/3/2026, 5:23:13 AM Updated 8/3/2026, 8:48:12 AM Related Associated Press AP World news Estonia Seto Kingdom Day Women wearing traditional Seto costumes dance during the annual Seto Kingdom Day in Mikitamäe, south Estonia, Saturday, Aug. 1, 2026. (AP Photo/Sergei Grits) By KOSTYA MANENKOV — Associated Press MIKITAMÄE, Estonia (AP) — As an accordion plays, 80-year-old Maime Kapten spins across the grass field, her embroidered skirt swirling and silver chains and coins around her neck jangling. Kapten is a member of the Seto ethnic community, which once a year turns a village in southeastern Estonia into a symbolic kingdom for a day — complete with entry visas instead of tickets, made-up currency and even a mock military parade. She's one of only a few thousand fluent speakers of Seto, which is closely related to the Estonian language. Other WRAL Top Stories The idea was born in 1994 as the Setos, whose homeland was divided by the Estonian-Russian border after the collapse of the Soviet Union, created a special event to highlight their unique culture and preserve their language, and bring the community together. “This is an important cultural day for us,” Kapten said. “We get to meet people we know, we get to talk, exchange a few words, give each other a hug.” The event brings together a far-flung community The Seto people have lived for centuries in the border region and never had a real kingdom. After the Soviet Union's collapse, many on the Russian side of the border eventually abandoned or sold their houses and moved to Estonia. Fewer than 200 stayed behind. Those who remained on the different sides of the border couldn’t see each other as easily as before and needed visas to visit family graves and relatives. According to Estonia's 2021 census, about 25,000 people reported being able to speak Seto, but linguists estimate only a few thousand use it in everyday life. Seto speakers are spread across Estonia, and the Setomaa parish in their traditional home region is home to fewer than 3,000 people. You'll hear a Seto woman before you see her The parish includes the usually quiet village of Mikitamäe, host to this year's kingdom day, whose streets were bursting on Saturday with men and women in colorful folk costumes. A local saying goes that you hear a Seto woman before you see her because of the noise her silver chains and dangling coins make. Those traditional dresses, worn every day a century ago, now are only worn for special occasions. “Seto clothes say a lot about the person who wears them,” said cultural activist Piret Torm-Kriis, 62. “If you look at a Seto woman, you can understand whether she is married or single, whether she is going to the church or to the market, to a party or to work.” Setos have a new community leader For centuries, Seto culture has combined Eastern Orthodox traditions and pre-Christian mythology. Setos attended church services but also sought help from Peko, the god of fertility and king of the Setos in local folklore. The tradition lives on with the annual election of a new Ülemsootska, the representative of the community, who speaks on Peko’s behalf and serves as his messenger. Each year, a man and a woman declare their program while standing on tree stumps to the Seto people, who quickly form lines in front of their favored candidate, holding onto threads stretching hundreds of meters (yards). On Saturday, the longest line formed in front of folk costume maker Ingrit Kala, who was declared the Ülemsootska. Topping Kala's agenda: promoting the Seto culture and preserving the Seto language. The language is officially viewed as a dialect of Estonian but considered a separate language by the Seto themselves, with its distinct pronunciation, grammar and vocabulary. “We have so many different things, so many skilled craftspeople, to show what a rich culture we have and to really introduce it,” Kala said. The Setos have a unique singing tradition Saturday's events prominently featured the traditional Seto way of singing, known as leelo, believed to be over 1,000 years old and recognized on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. It features a woman singing the first verse line, with a choir joining in for the final syllables before the singing blends together. Its lyrics and themes are often mythological and have been passed down orally from one generation to another. Singing traditionally accompanied all daily activities, with songs for everything, including work, rituals and celebrations. Leelo singing contains a lot of information about the world and people at the time of its origins, “how were they thinking, what was important, what did they believe in,” leelo singing researcher and teacher Mari Palolill said after singing with her choir. Setos face challenges in preserving their culture and language Seto traditions have survived largely by being passed on by word of mouth, and the annual kingdom day is one of the most important events for preserving the Seto language. In Setomaa, there is a Seto-speaking kindergarten group and a newspaper in Seto. Some books, including Antoine de Saint-Exupéry's “The Little Prince,” have been translated into Seto. Still, it remains a language largely learned in the family. “If Seto isn’t spoken at home, then what children learn at school doesn’t help much,” Kala said Maria Grünberg, 23, learned Seto by listening to leelo songs as a child and trying to sing along. Now she’s leading the youth leelo choir and her dream is to help every generation embrace Seto. “We all together try to preserve the songs, the language, and show also other young people that Seto songs and Seto language is not only for old people,” said Grünberg, who sang wearing a traditional Seto dress she customized herself and her grandparents' jewelry. “We want to show that this is for everyone.” Copyright 2026 by The Associated Press. https://www.baltictimes.com/lithuania_s_.text: Estonia Latvia Lithuania Business Analysis Opinions Culture EU Affairs Search Archive Lithuania's finance minister says diesel prices do not warrant emergency action 2026-08-05 BNS/TBT Staff VILNIUS - Lithuania's fuel market is not yet in a dramatic enough situation to warrant emergency intervention, Finance Minister Taurimas Valys said, as average diesel prices reached 2 euros per litre. Valys reiterated that measures would only be necessary if oil prices remained above 100 U.S. dollars per barrel for several consecutive days. On Tuesday, Brent crude was trading at 79.36 U.S. dollars per barrel. "We have certainly not reached any critical threshold now. Given the fluctuations seen today and last week, intervention is not always necessary. We do not see a dramatic situation at the moment," Valys told reporters on Wednesday. The minister said both tax and non-tax measures to mitigate prices had been "refined", but there was currently no basis for their implementation. Valys noted that one such measure would involve a reduction in fuel excise duties. According to the Lithuanian Energy Agency, the average price of diesel in Lithuania stands at 2.027 euros per litre, while petrol averages 1.778 euros. Prime Minister Mindaugas Sinkevicius previously said the government would take action to cushion the impact if high fuel prices persisted over a longer period. Energy Minister Lukas Savickas also said earlier that temporary price management measures would be considered if prices deviated from European or regional trends for an extended period. Following the outbreak of conflict in the Middle East in mid-April, Lithuania reduced the excise duty on diesel by 6 cents for two months. https://www.hellenicshippingnews.com/how.text: Odfjell SE 2Q26: A strong financial result Panama Canal Adopts Additional Measures to Address Reduced Precipitation in the Canal Watershed Xeneta weekly ocean container shipping market update – 21.08.26 Updated Implementing Regulation (EU) 2026/1434 amending the MED: In force from 31 August 2026 Baltic Dry Index Rises for 2nd Day, Still Posts Weekly Loss How Europe’s drought exposes ‘weakness of fossil fuels’ as Poland forced to shut down coal plants in Commodity News 10/08/2026 Poland has been forced to reduce output on its coal-fired power plants following critically low water levels in the Vistula River. Poland has been urged to double down on clean energy after Europe’s drought wreaked havoc on its coal industry. Earlier this week (4 August) utility giant Enea was forced to reduce generation at the Kozienice and Połaniec coal-fired power plants after critically low water levels in the Vistula River limited cooling water supplies. The move is said to have removed 1.3 GW from Poland’s power system, enough to power more than one million average households. This is around two per cent of the country’s current energy capacity. River flow near the Kozienice Power Plant fell to just 135 cubic metres per second on 5 August, reflecting severe drought conditions. The plant’s cooling system withdraws approximately 80–100 m³/s of water from the river – more than half of the remaining flow under such conditions. Despite growing evidence that the plant is killing millions of fish larvae, including from six protected species, Enea is cracking on with plans to build a near 1.3GW gas-fired power plant at the Kozienice site. Experts warn that such a move will increase pressure on the Vistula River ecosystem through continued high cooling water demand. ‘The paradox of the climate crisis’ “This is the paradox of the climate crisis: power plants driving climate change are increasingly becoming its victims,” says Paweł Pomian, Vice-President of Polish environmental organisation EKO-UNIA. “As the Vistula River dries up, an energy system built around large thermal power plants loses its resilience. Kozienice isn’t unique. There are many plants with similar cooling systems across Poland and there will be more if the government continues to expand fossil gas.” Pomian argues that Europe’s latest drought should be a “wake-up call” for Poland and the rest of the continent to transition towards technologies like solar and wind power that require the least amount of water to generate electricity. Poland urged to ditch coal Despite witnessing some of the most rapid growth in solar power in Europe – adding more than 20 GW of solar capacity between 2020 and 2025 – Poland’s combined share of wind and solar remains five per cent lower than the EU average. According to energy think tank Ember, Poland relies on coal for more than half (51 per cent) of its electricity – while wind and solar only make 25 per cent of the mix. Poland aims for 51 per cent of renewable electricity generation and 64 GW of renewable capacity by 2030, but its coal addiction is proving difficult to shake. Coal plants are paying the price for the problems they created,” says Kasia Szeniawska, a campaigner at Beyond Fossil Fuels. “As heatwaves and droughts become more severe, it has exposed the weakness of fossil fuel-based energy systems. While most EU countries cut down their coal use, Poland is not only failing a timely phase-out, it’s also proposing new gas plants that will only aggravate environmental issues.” Europe’s drought hits renewables Europe’s hot and dry summer, which climate scientists say would be “virtually impossible” if it wasn’t for the burning of fossil fuels, has also impacted the renewable energy sector. According to energy intelligence firm Montel, inflows to reservoirs and run-of-river hydropower plants in Austria and Switzerland were nearly 50 per cent below average in July. Total hydro production for Austria in July was only 51 per cent of normal levels (compared against the last 15 years) due to low rainfall, Montel adds. Similarly, Switzerland saw 48 per cent of normal production, while Germany (63 per cent) and France (68 per cent) also suffered. While significant drops in hydro output can push countries back onto polluting sources like coal, solar and wind can often compensate for the drop in electricity generation. For example, Ember says weather conditions caused a 12 per cent drop in annual hydropower production last year, contributing to gas generation in the EU rising by eight per cent (compared to 2024). However, the same weather conditions (which also caused wind power to fall by two per cent) boosted solar generation. This meant that in 2025, solar generated more EU power than ever before, growing by more than 20 per cent. It highlights the importance of diversifying the renewable energy mix in an era of climate-fuelled extreme weather. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/16/magy.text: Menü Kereső Magyar szerint akár pár hónap múlva folytathatják a tárgyalásokat Zelenszkijjel Belföld Flachner Balázs Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Volodimir Zelenszkij ukrán elnök után Magyar Péter miniszterelnök is megosztott néhány részletet kettejük pénteken lezajlott, négyszemközti tárgyalásáról . Magyar korábban már posztolt arról, hogy mikről egyeztettek Zelenszkijjel, de ebben nem írt arról, hogy szóba került volna a legmagasabb szintű találkozó terve, azaz olyan megbeszélés, ahol az egyik fél házigazdaként fogadja a másikat. Este az Egyenes Beszédben viszont említette ezt, mint mondta, abban maradtak, hogy most a miniszterek fogják azonosítani azokat a projekteket, ahol együtt tudnak működni, és ha ezek mennek, akkor pár hónap múlva jöhet egy találkozó Budapesten, Kijevben vagy Beregszászon. Magyar azt mondta, a találkozójukon alapvetően arról volt szó, hogy új alapokra kell helyezni a két ország kapcsolatát, amire szerinte most mindkét oldalról megvan a nyitottság. Rónai Egon felvetette, hogy ehhez erős gesztus lenne, ha Zelenszkij ott lenne az október 23-i ünnepségen, amire meg is hívták, sőt, az elnök korábban úgy reagált erre, hogy nincs ellene a dolognak, és azt kérdezte Magyartól, hogy szerinte eljön-e. Magyar erre annyit mondott, hogy minden állam- és kormányfőt meghívták az orosz elnököt leszámítva, és ő nem gondolja, hogy az ukrán elnök el fog jönni. Mint mondta, abban maradtak Zelenszkijjel, hogy mostantól a miniszterek fogják folytatni a tárgyalásokat. „Azonosítják Kárpátalján azokat a projekteket, legyen szó egy kórházról, iskoláról, vagy akár kölcsönös érdekeken nyugvó gazdasági projekteket, amikben tudunk előrelépni, és mi, hogyha ezek mennek, akkor majd pár hónap múlva találkozunk vagy Kijevben, vagy Beregszászon, vagy Budapesten, és folytatjuk ezeket a tárgyalásokat” – mondta Magyar. A miniszterelnök egyébként korábban is beszélt már arról, hogy egy ilyen találkozó lehetne Beregszászon. Zelenszkij a találkozó után azt írta, a kétoldalú kapcsolatok legfontosabb kérdéseiről egyeztetett Magyar Péterrel, emellett pedig Ukrajna uniós csatlakozásának előrehaladását is megvitatták. Az ukrán elnök szintén írt arról, hogy megállapodtak a közös munka különböző szinteken történő újraindításáról, és kölcsönös látogatásokat szerveznek majd, ezeknek a találkozóknak az időpontjait a két ország illetékes csapatai egyeztetik majd. Police threaten to arrest, prosecute persons destroying campaign posters, billboards The police said on Wednesday that it had observed growing incidents of deliberate tearing, defacement and destruction of campaign materials across the country. The police have warned politicians and their supporters against the destruction of campaign posters, banners and billboards belonging to rival candidates ahead of the 2027 general elections. Join the Premium Times WhatsApp Community For Quick Access To News and Happenings Around You. The police said on Wednesday that it had observed growing incidents of deliberate tearing, defacement and destruction of campaign materials across the country. The perpetrators will be arrested and prosecuted, the police said. In a statement issued on 4 November, police spokesperson Ani Iniedu said the practice constituted political intolerance. He urged those involved to desist immediately. The police said the destruction, defacement or unlawful removal of another candidate’s campaign materials could constitute malicious damage, a criminal offence under applicable laws, including Section 451 of the Criminal Code Act and Section 326 of the Penal Code Law. “Political differences or loyalty to a particular party do not give anyone the right to destroy another candidate’s property or infringe on their right to campaign freely,” the statement read. The police reiterated that all political parties and candidates, regardless of their affiliations or status, were entitled to equal protection under the law. They added that no individual or group had the right to determine whose campaign materials should be displayed or destroyed. Stay Ahead with Premium Times Follow us on Google News and never miss breaking stories, investigations, and in-depth reporting. According to the statement, the Inspector General of Police (IGP), Olatunji Disu, directed commissioners of police in the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory to take proactive measures to prevent such incidents, investigate reported cases, and ensure suspects are arrested and prosecuted. The police also warned that political sponsors and individuals who recruit, encourage or facilitate the destruction of campaign materials would be held accountable where evidence established their involvement. READ ALSO: Police uncover indoor cannabis farm in Lagos, arrest Polish, Nigerian nationals The police urged political parties, candidates, and their supporters to conduct their campaigns peacefully and respect others’ rights. They also warned that political intolerance, intimidation and criminal conduct must not undermine Nigeria’s democratic process. “The Nigeria Police Force will not allow political thugs and troublemakers to turn the nation’s political environment into a theatre of lawlessness,” the statement said. “Those who choose to break the law will face the full consequences of their actions.” PREMIUM TIMES reports that campaigns have started across the country, in preparation for the early 2027 general elections. https://www.euronews.com/2026/11/27/by-p.text: Belarusian President Aliaksandr Lukashenka has questioned the logic behind Russia's claims to Ukrainian territory on historical grounds, saying in an interview that following the same reasoning Russia itself should be returned to Mongolia.Speaking to French magazine Le Point, Lukashenka said that attempts to justify territorial claims by appealing to medieval history were misplaced, citing the period of Mongol domination over the Russian principalities between the 13th and late 15th centuries."And today to say that these lands are Russian and have been since time immemorial… At some point they were Russian. But if you look more deeply, Russian lands themselves were once Mongol-Tatar, remember? Then we should hand over the whole of Russia to whom, Mongolia?" Lukashenka said.He traced East Slavic statehood to the era of Kyivan Rus' in the 11th and 12th centuries — in what is now Ukraine — and said later historical periods could not be used to justify claims on today's independent states.Lukashenka then appeared to soften the remarks, insisting that Putin "perfectly understands this" and does not dispute the existence of the Ukrainian people or Ukrainian statehood, and that he is simply "misinterpreted".He added that he shares Moscow's position on "the need for a common future for the peoples of the region."The remarks echo a 2024 post by former Mongolian president Tsakhiagiin Elbegdorj, who published a "Mongolian historical map" from 1471 on X after Putin gave US conservative journalist Tucker Carlson an extended account of Russian history, showing a diminished Russia within a vast Mongol domain."Don't worry. We are a peaceful and free nation," Elbegdorj wrote.History of ahistorical claimsPutin's argument that parts of Ukraine are "primordially Russian" has been central to the Kremlin's official rhetoric since his 2021 article "On the Historical Unity of Russians and Ukrainians".On the eve of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine on 24 February 2022, Putin invoked those historical claims explicitly, using them to deny Ukraine's legitimacy as an independent state and to frame the invasion as a correction of a historical injustice.Historians and international observers have described the Kremlin's attempt to use this precedent as selective and ahistorical.Lukashenka has ruled Belarus since 1994, making him Europe's longest-serving leader. Following a disputed 2020 presidential election that triggered mass protests and a violent crackdown, he relied on the Kremlin's support to remain in power.The EU and Western governments did not recognise the election result. Thousands of protesters were arrested, and opposition figures were imprisoned or forced into exile.Belarus allowed Russia to use its territory to launch parts of its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, with Russian forces advancing toward Kyiv from the north before being repelled.Minsk has since remained a close military and political ally of Moscow, although it has stopped short of committing its own troops to the war.Belarus has faced successive rounds of Western sanctions over both the crackdown on dissent and its role in the war.
